title: Information locality of a quantum locally recoverable code
abstract: A classical linear code $C$ of length $n$ is said to have symbol locality $(r, δ)$ if for any index $j$ there exists a repair group $J_j \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n\}$ with $j\in J_j$ and $|J_j| \leq r+δ-1$ such that any $δ-1$ or fewer erasures in $J_j$ can be corrected by using codeword symbols only in $J_j$. Later it turned out that this way of defining $r$ overestimates the number of necessary codeword symbols for multiple-erasure correction, and information locality was proposed to define $r$ as the dimension of the punctured code of $C$ onto $J_j$. Recently locality $(r,δ)$ was proposed for quantum error-correcting codes by following the original definition of symbol locality $(r, δ)$. We propose a quantum counterpart of the information locality for quantum stabilizer codes constructed by Hermitian orthogonality, and a linear algebraic procedure computing a smaller repair group predicted by the proposed information locality and simultaneously reducing the number of measured observables in decoding to its minimum possible value. Then we demonstrate that the previously proposed definition of quantum locality $(r,δ)$ has the same drawback of overestimating the number of necessary codeword symbols for erasure correction by providing an explicit example of a quantum stabilizer code. Finally, we will give another example of a quantum stabilizer code constructed by Euclidean orthogonality and two different linear codes, with which a natural translation of the classical information locality into the quantum setting underestimates the number of necessary codeword symbols for erasure correction.
summary: This paper introduces a refined concept called 'information locality' for Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECCs) to improve upon existing overestimations of required resources for erasure correction. Using advanced linear algebra on code subspaces, the authors derive constructive methods and prove that their proposed measure yields tighter bounds than previous quantum locality definitions. This work is vital for designing efficient and resource-aware fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a quantum counterpart of 'information locality' for Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECCs) to provide a more accurate measure of the necessary codeword symbols required for erasure correction than existing methods.
main_result: The proposed information locality definition is shown to be superior to previous definitions by providing tighter bounds, although limitations exist when applying it to general QECCs beyond stabilizer codes.
method: The authors use linear algebraic procedures involving punctured and shortened code constructions ($\pi_J(C)$ and $\sigma_J(C^{\perp} \otimes h)$) to derive and compare different locality parameters for quantum stabilizer codes.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECCs), specifically stabilizer codes $Q(C)$, which are complex subspaces of the tensor product Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}^{\otimes n}_{\mathbb{C}_q}$. The analysis involves local measurements and recovery procedures.
key_observables: Locality parameters $(r, \delta)$; dimension of punctured/shortened codes ($\dim \pi_J(C)$); minimum Hamming weights ($w_H$); quantum local distance ($\delta_Q$).
important_parameters: Code length $n$, code dimension $k$; field size $q$; locality parameters $(r, \delta)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on the structure of stabilizer codes and specific linear algebraic decompositions; limitations are noted when assuming general QECCs or when comparing classical vs. quantum settings.
paper_structure: The paper reviews classical locality definitions, proposes a quantum information locality based on punctured code dimensions, develops constructive proofs (Propositions 1 and 7) to compute the required repair group size, compares this new measure against symbol locality, and finally discusses limitations using counterexamples.
why_interesting: It advances the theoretical understanding of fault-tolerance in quantum computation by refining the metrics used to quantify local error correction capabilities, which is crucial for building scalable quantum hardware.
